subtitle:
My AI journey. A little Web3.
Something you can actually build.
label: A hands-on workshop · Avalanche Fuji
notes: Welcome people who have never coded as well as people who have. This is a live workshop, not a promise that AI makes software risk-free. The goal is a small working dApp and a repeatable way to direct an agent.

title: Three parts. One working app.
items: 20 min · chat → coding agents → agent workspaces
25 min · shared records, wallets and transactions
footer: Keep 10 minutes for questions and troubleshooting.
notes: Suggested two-hour pacing, assuming tools are installed before the workshop. The repository's original station timetable is different; this deck deliberately follows the presenter's three-part talk. Use fallback art and a facilitator demonstration if setup consumes build time.

title: What an agent workspace helps organize
right: Is the result ready to use?
footer: Tools such as Zcode · the general idea is a workspace for coding agents
notes: The presenter currently uses Zcode or ADE-like workspaces. Describe the category, not a product tutorial or endorsement. Do not promise a particular feature in every tool.

title: The habit worth learning
footer: You can begin without knowing every line of code.
notes: Explain that directing and evaluating remain learnable skills. Technical knowledge helps you ask better questions and recognize failure. Ask the audience what tiny thing they would like to build.

title:
What happens
after you click?
subtitle: Enough blockchain to understand your first dApp.
notes: Bridge from AI to the software we are going to build. Avoid a long history of cryptocurrencies or investment discussion.

title: A familiar website
footer: Usually, an organization operates the service and its database.
notes: Use a familiar example such as a loyalty-point balance. This is a simplified web application; not every system has exactly three components.

title: A blockchain is a shared record
subtitle: Many computers check updates using common rules.
footer: A public record can be checked beyond one website.
notes: Blocks connect to earlier blocks using cryptographic references. Nodes maintain and verify the chain under a consensus protocol. A blockchain does not prove that every real-world claim written into it is true. Public addresses are pseudonymous, not automatically private.

title: A transaction requests a change
footer: A transaction hash identifies the request. A successful receipt confirms its outcome.
notes: Sending a request is not the same as success. It may be rejected, remain pending or execute and revert. An included failed transaction can still consume gas. Our app waits for a receipt before reporting a successful mint.

title: A smart contract holds the rules
subtitle: Think of a vending machine with inspectable instructions.
items: Request one NFT and pay the mint price
Correct payment? Supply available? Not paused?
Create a token and record its owner
footer: The rules are code. Code can contain mistakes.
notes: The vending-machine analogy is limited: a smart contract executes in the blockchain environment. This repository uses a non-upgradeable contract; changing its bytecode requires a new deployment. Its owner can still change settings explicitly exposed by the code, such as pause and the metadata base URI. Avoid saying every blockchain contract is immutable in every possible sense.

title: Proof of stake: who helps validate?
items: Check blocks and participate in consensus
footer: Exact rewards and penalties depend on the network.
notes: Keep this conceptual. Proof of stake is about participation and economic security; a separate consensus protocol determines agreement. Do not teach Ethereum's specific penalties as universal Avalanche behavior. We are not setting up validators or staking funds in this workshop.

title: Avalanche: ask a sample, repeat
subtitle: Validators repeatedly sample other validators to reach agreement.
footer: Simplified view of Snowman consensus · valid blocks only
notes: Advance through the highlighted nodes. This is an illustrative diagram, not a simulation of protocol thresholds or timing. Stake influences participation; repeated sampling is the agreement mechanism. Invalid transactions are not made valid by votes. Omit performance numbers and detailed parameters.

title: Our classroom: Avalanche Fuji
items: The test network we use today
The chain ID to check in your wallet
footer: Gas is paid in test AVAX. No real funds needed.
notes: Ethereum compatibility lets us use familiar Solidity contracts, ethers and wallet tooling. Fuji is a separate test network. A chain ID tells the app which chain is selected; an address alone does not identify a network. Network details are listed in the appendix.

title: Your wallet is a key manager
footer: MetaMask is one way to interact with your accounts.
notes: For the account model used in this workshop, the private key authorizes signatures. The wallet displays chain data; the NFT is not a picture stored inside the wallet. Never ask anyone to show a secret or recovery phrase during the demonstration.

title: Public address. Private control.
right: Never paste a recovery phrase into AI
Never share your main-wallet private key
footer: The deploy lesson uses a separate, fresh testnet-only burner.
notes: The recovery phrase can restore control over accounts; the app does not need it. The only taught file-based key exception is a fresh disposable testnet-only burner in gitignored foundry/.env. Do not display the .env file in the presentation or screen share. This deck does not connect to a wallet.

title: Three requests. Different meanings.
items: Share the selected account with the site.
Authorize or attest to the displayed message.
Request an on-chain action; gas may be charged.
footer: Read every request. A gas-free signature can still grant important permissions.
notes: Connecting alone is not a token-spending approval. Message signatures can have consequences, including authorizing later actions. Disconnecting a dApp does not revoke previously granted token approvals. Our NFT mint uses native test AVAX rather than an ERC-20 allowance.

title: One mint, step by step
footer: Use Next to reveal each step. This is an illustration, not a real transaction.
notes: Walk through the same journey students will perform. Between the wallet and chain, an RPC endpoint relays requests. The app then reads updated contract data. No wallet connection or network transaction happens in this slide.

title: Mint price and gas are different
footer: Two NFTs cost 0.02 test AVAX plus gas. Gas varies.
notes: The contract requires the exact mint payment for the chosen quantity. The wallet estimates the network fee separately. Rejecting a wallet request before broadcast does not send a transaction; a transaction included but reverted can still consume gas.

title: Checkpoint: get ready to build
items: Use a workshop account; keep recovery information private.
Use the faucet and check your balance.
footer: faucet.avax.network · backup: faucets.chain.link/fuji
notes: Pause here. Install MetaMask only through its official website and official extension-store listing. Follow docs/02-fuji-faucet.md for setup. Faucet availability and eligibility may vary; ask a facilitator if blocked. Never buy real tokens for this workshop.

title:
Make something
you can use.
subtitle: A small NFT minting app. A repeatable way to build.
notes: Show the destination before the tools. If possible, briefly demonstrate a working facilitator dApp in a separate browser tab.

title: Your first dApp
subtitle: A minting page for your own collection.
items: A receipt and your owned tokens
footer: 100 tokens maximum · 0.01 test AVAX each · Fuji only
notes: The visual is a conceptual preview using the repository's fallback art, not a screenshot or a live mint interface. The existing app has a gallery, quantity selector, minted count and My NFTs. Contract address wiring is required before a real mint. Artwork display additionally depends on reachable metadata.

title: The pieces you are connecting
footer: Foundry builds, tests and deploys the contract.
notes: A dApp means decentralized application, but not every part is decentralized. The website and metadata can still use ordinary hosting. ethers talks to the blockchain through an RPC provider and requests wallet signing for transactions. Foundry is development tooling, not part of the user's mint click.

title:
ERC = Ethereum
Request for Comments
subtitle: Shared standards help different apps speak the same language.
footer: 20 and 721 identify different standards, not software versions.
notes: ERCs are a category of standards proposals. ERC-20 and ERC-721 define common token interfaces. Ethereum-compatible chains such as Avalanche C-Chain can implement them too. A standard helps compatibility; it does not guarantee safety, value or support in every wallet.

title: ERC-20: interchangeable units
subtitle: Like points in the same loyalty program.
footer: The question is “how much?” · units of the same token are interchangeable
notes: The analogy is to units within one token contract; different ERC-20 tokens are not interchangeable with each other. ERC-20 includes balance, transfer and allowance interfaces. This repository has WorkToken as an optional extension, not the main build.

title: ERC-721: individually identified tokens
subtitle: Like numbered tickets, each with its own identity.
footer: The question is “which one?” · contract address + token ID identify the NFT on a chain
notes: NFT means non-fungible token. ERC-721 tracks and transfers ownership of individual token IDs. Images are commonly referenced through metadata and are not necessarily stored on-chain. NFT ownership does not automatically transfer copyright or guarantee the truth of a real-world claim.

title: Which standard fits?
right: An owner for each token ID
footer: Choose the behavior first. Choose the standard second.
notes: Ask the audience to classify loyalty points and numbered collectibles. Do not introduce prices or trading. The main workshop stays with ERC-721.

title: Your conversation has a structure
items: Agree how to approach the work
footer: Start from a requirements brief. Keep the spec open beside your AI chat.
notes: Facilitator transition: “You will spend this part talking to your own agent. These slides are signposts. Stay on the phase you are working on; you do not need to keep pace with every slide.” Requirements come before the four speckit phases. Verification happens within implementation and at the final checklist; it is not an invented fifth speckit command. Let students keep their attention on their own screens.

title: First, understand the requirements
items: Ask your agent to explain requirements/R2-mint-dapp.md.
The acceptance criteria are your checklist for success.
You choose the layout, wording and visual details.
footer: Your screen: the requirements brief + your AI conversation.
notes: Leave this slide up while learners read, roughly 3 minutes. Say: “The requirements tell you what the client needs. The open questions are your decisions. Ask your agent to explain anything unclear before it writes code.” Circulate and ask one learner to name a required behavior and one choice they control. Keep all acceptance criteria; do not let the agent silently simplify them. If using starter art temporarily, record it as unfinished against the brief rather than marking the art requirement complete.

title: Specify: answer before building
quote: Run the speckit.specify prompt for requirements/R2-mint-dapp.md. Ask me the open questions one at a time. Write my answers into speckit/specs/build-spec.md, then wait for my confirmation.
footer: Checkpoint: “This spec describes what I want.”
notes: Leave up while learners talk with their agents, roughly 7 minutes. Say: “Give your own answers. If the agent chooses for you, ask it to come back to the question. You can ask what a word means.” The learner must provide at least three answers before the spec is written. Have them read the finished spec, including unchanged acceptance criteria, and confirm it. A chat reply saying “done” is not the specification. The actual file is the agreement.

title: Plan: understand the approach
quote: Run the speckit.plan prompt using my confirmed speckit/specs/build-spec.md. Explain the files, tools and order of work in plain language. Show me the plan before changing code.
footer: Checkpoint: “I understand what will change and why.”
notes: Leave up for roughly 3 minutes. Say: “You do not need to recognize every filename. Ask what each part is responsible for. If the plan adds a feature you never requested, bring it back to your spec.” The repository plan prompt refers to an older station-specs path, so this prompt explicitly supplies the actual build-spec path. The agent shows a short plan and gets a go-ahead. If the plan reveals a requirement problem, update the spec before proceeding.

title: Tasks: make progress checkable
quote: Run the speckit.tasks prompt for my approved plan. Make small tasks with something I can check after each one. Start by showing the current app. End with my spec’s verification checklist. Show me the list, then stop.
footer: Checkpoint: every task tells you what to look at.
notes: Leave up for roughly 3 minutes. Say: “A good task ends with something you can see: an image, a button, a message or a receipt. If a task says only ‘finish the app’, ask for smaller tasks.” Learners should review the checklist before asking for implementation. The tasks phase does not automatically authorize code changes. Use the pause to ask students how they will recognize success.

title: Implement: one result at a time
quote: Run the speckit.implement prompt for my approved spec, plan and tasks. After each task, show me the real result and tell me what to check. If something fails, explain it and propose the smallest fix.
footer: Your screen: the running app + the task checklist + your AI chat.
notes: Keep this slide up during the main work period, roughly 15 minutes. Say occasionally: “Which task are you on? What changed on the page? Can you show the result?” The agent handles setup commands, starting the app and appropriate checks. Learners inspect the actual result rather than copy terminal commands from the projector. The agent marks implemented tasks, but a checked task is not a substitute for the learner verifying it. Do not talk continuously; leave quiet time for their conversations.

title: Check the result against your spec
items: Ask the agent to show where it is satisfied.
Check the artwork, wallet connection, quantity and error states.
Keep failed or blocked items open, with the next action.
footer: “Which requirement does this prove?” is better than “Is it done?”
notes: Leave up during verification, roughly 5 minutes. Say: “Do not accept a confident paragraph as proof. Open the page and try the behavior.” Ask the agent: “Walk me through every acceptance criterion. Show evidence and tell me what is incomplete.” Minting remains blocked until the contract is deployed and wired. The agent runs the relevant automated checks, including contract tests before deployment, and explains results against the rules. Passing tests does not replace visual and on-chain evidence or constitute a security audit. Learners verify and tick their spec checklist.

title: Refine the conversation
right: Preserve the image proportions. Change only this.
Check the Fuji-only requirement. Show the fix and verify it again.
footer: Observation → expected result → smallest change → recheck the same criterion.
notes: Use this while learners iterate, roughly 4 minutes or as needed. Say: “Describe the difference between your spec and the screen. Point to the exact thing you want changed.” Ask whether the learner is fixing an implementation or changing a requirement. If they want a new behavior, update the spec and plan first; if the agreed behavior is broken, repair the relevant task and recheck. Avoid silently expanding scope.

title: Next brief: deploy and connect
quote: Read requirements/R3-go-live.md and the deploy guide. Use speckit to specify and plan my Fuji deployment and wiring. Explain the contract rules, run the required checks, and show me the results before I approve deployment.
footer: Fresh testnet burner only · Fuji 43113 · tests pass before deployment.
notes: Introduce the next brief once the frontend checkpoint is reached, roughly 5 minutes for specification and planning. Repeat specify → plan → tasks → implement for the wiring spec rather than skipping the method. R3 contains an older manual-command ritual; this workshop follows AGENTS.md’s agent-run command playbook with the learner making decisions and explicitly approving the broadcast. The agent explains rules such as 0.01 test AVAX per NFT, maximum supply 100 and quantity 1–5, runs contract tests and shows their results. Guide fresh testnet-burner setup privately using docs/05-deploy-foundry.md section 0. Only that disposable key goes in gitignored foundry/.env. Never request or project a recovery phrase, main-wallet key or .env contents. The agent wires the public deployed address after approval; no manual config editing is required from learners.

title: Finish with evidence, not a promise
items: Understand the checks and approve before the agent broadcasts.
Read MetaMask before approving the mint request.
Check the successful receipt and your token ownership.
footer: Ask your agent to explain what each piece of evidence proves.
notes: Allow roughly 15 minutes for deployment, wiring and proof; use the remaining build time as buffer. Say: “Your agent can do the technical steps. You still decide whether to approve, and you inspect the result.” Ask the agent to guide each verification item from the actual wiring spec. Check the Fuji receipt, contract address, mint recipient and token. A missing image or wallet display is still an open acceptance item; ownership and metadata availability are different checks. The agent can diagnose and explain the smallest fix. Do not mark all requirements complete just because one transaction succeeded.

title: If you get stuck, keep talking
quote: I am on this task: ___. I expected ___. What I see is ___. Help me understand the difference. Propose the smallest fix, then show me how to verify it against my spec.
footer: Ask for an explanation. Share the error text, never secrets. Call a helper when needed.
notes: Use this as a holding slide while circulating. Say: “Being stuck is a useful moment to practice giving context. Tell your agent which task you are on and what you expected.” If it repeatedly fails, ask it to explain the evidence and narrow the problem before trying again. Invite learners who finish early to explain one acceptance check to a neighbor. If tooling blocks someone, let them observe a facilitator demonstration without pretending their own spec is complete.

title:
You direct.
The agent builds.
You verify.
subtitle: Today: one small dApp. Next: your own idea.
footer: Describe → build → inspect → refine
notes: Ask someone to explain one requirement, the conversation that turned it into a spec, and the evidence that convinced them it worked. Invite learners to share their collection and successful Fuji transaction. The transferable skill is directing work through requirements, spec, plan, tasks and verification. Optional next steps are separate briefs for WorkToken or hosting, with explicit approvals.
